proofs.proof_tex:
Fix an arbitrary finite scenario list \(\mathcal H_0=\{h^1,\ldots,h^M\}\subset[-H,H]^K\).  The proof below uses only this finiteness and the coordinate bound \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); it never invokes coordinatewise null-boundary closure.

\emph{Exact embedding.}
Fix \(n\) and \(\pi_n\in\Pi_n\).  On
\(((i-1)/n,i/n]\), let the continuous control be the vertex
\[
u_j(t)=\mathbf 1\{A_i=j\}.
\]
The action \(A_i\) is chosen at the left endpoint from the observed past.  It is therefore predictable by Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}finite\mbox{-}predictability}\), and the resulting piecewise-constant control belongs to \(\mathcal U\) by Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}continuous\mbox{-}observed\mbox{-}control}\) and Definition
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\).
Conditionally on the history and \(A_i=j\), its score increment is
\[
\Delta X_j=\frac{h_j^m}{n}
+W_j(i/n)-W_j((i-1)/n)
\sim\mathcal N(h_j^m/n,1/n),
\]
and its clock increment is \(1/n\); all other coordinates have zero
increments.  By Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}gaussian\mbox{-}known\mbox{-}variance}\)
and \(\mathrm{ass{:}local\mbox{-}scenario\mbox{-}scaling}\),
\(Y_i/\sqrt n\) has exactly this conditional law.  Induction over \(i\)
therefore gives equality of the complete observed score-clock laws under every
scenario \(m\), not merely weak convergence.  Thus every finite policy is a
vertex-control diffusion policy and has exactly the same scenario-risk vector.

\emph{Approximation for continuous terminal payoffs.}
Let \(g_m:\mathbb R^K\times[0,1]^K\to[0,1]\) be bounded and continuous,
for \(m=1,\ldots,M\).  We show that the infimal prior-weighted risk over the
embedded \(n\)-grid controls converges to the infimum over \(\mathcal U\).

On the canonical observed space, every progressively measurable
\(\Delta(\mathcal J)\)-valued control is approximable in
\(dt\,d\mathbb P_0\)-measure by simple predictable controls: approximate
indicators in the predictable sigma-field by finite unions of left-cylinder
sets, approximate the bounded simplex coordinates by simple functions, and
project onto the closed simplex.  Boundedness upgrades convergence in measure
to
\[
\mathbb E_0\int_0^1\sum_j|u_j^{(r)}(t)-u_j(t)|\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{1}
\]
For a fixed simple control, subdivide each of its time cells into \(n\)-grid
cells and, conditionally on the information at the left endpoint, choose
vertex \(j\) with its declared simplex probability.  The sum of the conditional
variances of the normalized centered allocation counts is at most \(1/n\), so
the cumulative clock error tends to zero in probability.  Conditional on
those counts, the score increment in coordinate \(j\) is Gaussian with mean
\(h_j^m\Delta Q_j\) and variance \(\Delta Q_j\).  Therefore its conditional
characteristic function is
\[
\exp\!\left\{\mathrm i z_jh_j^m\Delta Q_j
-\frac12z_j^2\Delta Q_j\right\},
\]
which converges to the characteristic function of the corresponding relaxed
Gaussian transition.  Induction over the finitely many simple-control cells
proves joint convergence of the terminal score and clock.  Past-measurable
simple functions may be chosen continuous outside sets of arbitrarily small
probability simultaneously under the finitely many scenario laws; changing
them on those sets changes a bounded risk by at most that probability.  A
diagonal choice in \(r\) and \(n\) therefore gives grid policies
\(\pi_n[u]\) such that
\[
(X_n,Q_n)\ \Longrightarrow\ (X^u(1),Q^u(1))
\quad\text{under every }m.
\tag{2}
\]
This construction uses vertex choices even when some simplex coordinates
are zero, so it imposes no exploration lower bound.

The transfer from the zero-drift reference law to every scenario is uniform.
The assignment factors cancel because the policy is scenario independent,
and the Gaussian likelihood ratio is
\[
Z_m(X,Q)=
\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j-\frac12
\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j\right\}.
\tag{3}
\]
Conditioning successively on score increments gives
\[
\mathbb E_0[Z_m(X,Q)^2]
=\mathbb E_0\exp\!\left\{\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j\right\}
\leq\exp(H^2),
\tag{4}
\]
because \(\sum_jQ_j=1\) and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\).  Thus the likelihood ratios
are uniformly integrable, and reference-law convergence transfers to all
\(M\) scenario laws.  Equations (1)--(4), bounded continuity of \(g_m\),
and an arbitrarily near-optimal choice of \(u\) show, for every
\(\lambda\in\Delta_M\),
\[
\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^{\pi_n}g_m
\longrightarrow
\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_m\mathbb E_m^ug_m.
\tag{5}
\]
The lower-bound direction in (5) holds for every \(n\), because exact
embedding makes the finite grid class a subclass of the continuous-control
class.  Hence this regular-payoff approximation is derived from the primitive
Gaussian transitions.

For fixed \(\delta>0\), the functions
\(\ell_{m,\delta}^{\pm}\) in Definition
\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\) are bounded and continuous:
exponentiation, finite averages, and finite minima are continuous, as are
\(f_\delta^\pm\).  Applying (5) yields
\[
B_{n,\delta}^\pm(\lambda)\longrightarrow
B_\delta^\pm(\lambda).
\tag{6}
\]
Every value in (6) is \(1\)-Lipschitz in \(\lambda\) for the
\(\ell_1\) norm, because every scenario risk is in \([0,1]\).  Cover compact
\(\Delta_M\) by a finite \(\ell_1\)-net, apply pointwise convergence at the
net points, and use the two Lipschitz bounds.  This upgrades (6) to convergence
uniform in \(\lambda\).

\emph{Removal of the continuous envelopes.}
The scalar bracketing in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) gives
\[
B_{n,\delta}^-(\lambda)\leq B_n(\lambda)\leq
B_{n,\delta}^+(\lambda),
\qquad
B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda).
\]
Combining these inequalities with uniform convergence in (6) gives
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
\leq\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta).
\]
Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) and using the final conclusion of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\) proves
\[
\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{7}
\]
For the point-mass prior \(e_m\), the definitions give
\(B_n(e_m)=c_{n,m}\) and \(B(e_m)=c_m\).  Hence (7) proves
\[
\max_{1\leq m\leq M}|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0.
\tag{8}
\]

For completeness, we derive the finite-scenario minimax identity needed to
pass from (7)--(8) to regret values.  Let \(C_n\) be the closure in
\([0,1]^M\) of the achievable regret vectors.  Independent randomization at
time zero makes it convex, and closure makes it compact without changing the
infimum of a continuous criterion.  Since
\(\max_m r_m=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\lambda^\top r\), finite-dimensional
convex separation gives
\[
\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m
=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\inf_{r\in C_n}\lambda^\top r.
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, let \(v=\inf_{r\in C_n}\max_mr_m\).  The upward-closed convex set
\(C_n+\mathbb R_+^M\) has \(v\mathbf1\) on its boundary.  Projecting
\((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto this set and taking a convergent subsequence of
the normalized projection normals produces \(\lambda\geq0\),
\(\sum_m\lambda_m=1\), with \(\lambda^\top r\geq v\) for every
\(r\in C_n\).  The opposite inequality follows from
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\), proving (9).
Translating from regret to loss yields
\[
V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}
\left\{B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}\right\},
\]
and the identical argument gives the corresponding formula for \(V\).
Consequently,
\[
|V_n-V|
\leq\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|
+\max_m|c_{n,m}-c_m|\longrightarrow0
\]
by (7)--(8).

\emph{Predictable policy attainment.}
Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  Choose \(N\) so large that
\(|V_N-V|+\max_m|c_{N,m}-c_m|<\epsilon/3\), and choose
\(\pi_N\in\Pi_N\) with
\[
\max_m\{L_N(\pi_N,m)-c_{N,m}\}\leq V_N+\epsilon/3.
\]
Embed \(\pi_N\) as the \(N\)-block vertex control \(u^\epsilon\) constructed
above.  Exact equality of risk vectors and the preceding bounds show
\[
\max_m r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon.
\tag{10}
\]
Thus \(u^\epsilon\) is an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.

It remains to approximate this particular control for the original
discontinuous loss.  Conditional on an exogenous random seed and on any of
the finitely many action sequences of \(\pi_N\), the sampled Gaussian block
increments have a Lebesgue density.  Every terminal threshold equality is
contained in a finite union of zero sets of
\[
\sum_{j\in I}\exp(X_j-Q_j/2)-20|I|.
\]
This analytic function is nonconstant whenever one of its coordinates was
sampled; if none was sampled, its value is \(|I|-20|I|\neq0\).
Its zero set therefore has Lebesgue measure zero.  Hence
\[
\Pr_m^{u^\epsilon}\{a_j(X(1),Q(1))=0
\text{ for some }j\}=0
\quad\text{for every }m.
\tag{11}
\]
At horizon \(n\), divide enrollment into \(N\) consecutive blocks whose
lengths differ from \(n/N\) by at most one, keep the arm selected by
\(\pi_N\) throughout a block, and feed the next decision the normalized
block aggregate.  This is a predictable finite policy.  Each aggregate is
exactly Gaussian with clock length converging to \(1/N\); induction over the
fixed number \(N\) of blocks gives convergence of its terminal state to that
of \(u^\epsilon\).  Arbitrary measurable recruitment kernels of \(\pi_N\)
may first be changed on sets of arbitrarily small probability under the
finite family of Gaussian history laws so that this induction is valid at
their continuity points.  Equation (11) then permits the bounded
continuous-mapping argument for the strict miss indicators.  Thus the
resulting predictable policies \(\pi_n^\epsilon\) satisfy
\[
L_n(\pi_n^\epsilon,m)\longrightarrow L(u^\epsilon,m)
\quad\text{for every }m.
\]
Together with (10), this proves the asserted coordinatewise risk transfer.
The construction admits zero block allocations to unused subgroups.  Every
argument above is internal to the declared finite list \(\mathcal H_0\);
the common-drift perturbation used by the terminal-comparison lemma is only a
change-of-measure device and does not require any translated or projected
scenario to belong to that list.

Fix either the finite experiment or the diffusion experiment, and write
\(\mathcal A\) for its policy class.  Use \(n\)-subscripts in the finite
case, and define
\[
r(a)=(L(a,1)-c_1,\ldots,L(a,M)-c_M)\in[0,1]^M.
\]
The inclusion in the cube follows because \(c_m\) is the infimum of the
\([0,1]\)-valued scenario risk, so \(0\leq L(a,m)-c_m\leq1\).
Let
\[
C:=\overline{\{r(a):a\in\mathcal A\}}\subset[0,1]^M.
\]
Time-zero randomization, allowed by Definitions
\(\mathrm{def{:}finite\mbox{-}policy\mbox{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}continuous\mbox{-}control\mbox{-}class}\), makes \(C\)
convex; it is compact by construction.

Put \(v=\min_{r\in C}\max_mr_m\).  The set
\(D=C+\mathbb R_+^M\) is closed and convex, and \(v\mathbf1\) is a boundary
point of \(D\).  Compactness supplies \(r^\star\in C\) with
\(r^\star\leq v\mathbf1\), whereas \((v-a)\mathbf1\notin D\) for every
\(a>0\).  Project \((v-k^{-1})\mathbf1\) onto \(D\).  The projection
inequality, followed by normalization and passage to a subsequence, supplies
a nonzero supporting normal \(\lambda^\star\).  Because \(D\) is upward
closed, every coordinate of this normal is nonnegative; normalize it so that
\(\sum_m\lambda_m^\star=1\).  The support inequality is
\[
\lambda^{\star\top}r\geq
\lambda^{\star\top}(v\mathbf1)=v
\quad\text{for every }r\in C.
\tag{12}
\]
Conversely, for every \(\lambda\in\Delta_M\),
\(\lambda^\top r\leq\max_mr_m\), whence
\[
\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\min_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r=v.
\tag{13}
\]
No regularity of the terminal loss was used in this finite-dimensional
separation.

Closure does not alter the infimum of a linear functional.  In the finite
experiment,
\[
\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r
=\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_m\lambda_m
\{L_n(\pi_n,m)-c_{n,m}\}
=B_n(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{n,m}.
\]
The same calculation with \(u\in\mathcal U\) gives
\(B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m\).  Substitution in (13) proves both
displayed minimax identities.  Moreover,
\[
\left|\inf_{r\in C}\lambda^\top r-
\inf_{r\in C}{\lambda'}^\top r\right|
\leq\sup_{r\in[0,1]^M}|(\lambda-\lambda')^\top r|
\leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
\]
Thus the dual objective is continuous on compact \(\Delta_M\), so a
least-favorable prior is attained in both experiments.

We next identify the sufficient posterior state.  Fix a prior \(\lambda\).
Under the zero-drift reference law and any scenario-independent observed
control, conditional Gaussian integration gives the likelihood ratio
\[
Z_m(X(t),Q(t))
=\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}.
\tag{14}
\]
The denominator \(\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r\) is strictly positive because every
\(Z_r>0\) and at least one \(\lambda_r>0\).  Bayes' formula gives
\[
\Pr\{m\mid\mathcal F_t\}
=\frac{\lambda_mZ_m(X(t),Q(t))}
{\sum_r\lambda_rZ_r(X(t),Q(t))}
=b_m^\lambda(X(t),Q(t)).
\tag{15}
\]
The same likelihood identity yields
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mL(u,m)
=\mathbb E_0^u\!\left[
\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m(X(1),Q(1))\ell_m(X(1),Q(1))
\right].
\tag{16}
\]
Thus the Bayes problem is a terminal-cost Markov problem in
\((t,X,Q,b^\lambda)\), with \(b^\lambda\) the deterministic function in
(15).

Markovization is direct in this Gaussian model.  For a relaxed observed
control, disintegrate its action at time \(t\) conditionally on
\((X(t),Q(t),b^\lambda(t))\), and use that conditional simplex vector as
the randomized Markov action.  For simple controls, iterated conditional
Gaussian kernels show by induction that this operation preserves the
terminal reference-law distribution.  Approximation by simple predictable
controls, using the bound
\[
\sup_{u,m}\mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))^2]\leq e^{H^2}
\tag{17}
\]
derived in the proof of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}boundary\mbox{-}stable\mbox{-}frontier}\), extends the
identity to all admissible relaxed controls.  Equations (14)--(17) then
show that it preserves every scenario risk, not merely the Bayes average.
Consequently Bayes responses may be chosen Markov in the state displayed in
the theorem.

Choose an attained least-favorable prior \(\lambda^\star\) for the diffusion
experiment.  We record why diffusion Bayes minimizers exist despite the
discontinuous payoff.  The cumulative
clock paths are uniformly \(1\)-Lipschitz and take values in a compact
simplex; the score martingales have uniformly bounded quadratic variation.
The induced relaxed-control laws are therefore tight.  Every weak limit
retains the Gaussian martingale problem because the drift and covariance
coefficients are bounded and affine in the relaxed action.  The map
\((x,q)\mapsto a_j(x,q)\) is continuous, hence
\(\mathbf1\{a_j(x,q)<0\}\) is lower semicontinuous.  The positive likelihood
weights in (16) are continuous, and the summands are nonnegative.  The
Portmanteau inequality applied term by term therefore shows that the Bayes
terminal cost is lower semicontinuous along relaxed-control limits.  A
minimizing sequence consequently has a minimizing relaxed-control limit;
Markovization then provides a Markov Bayes best response.

The same compactness argument applies to the finite maximum of the
lower-semicontinuous scenario regrets, so there is an attained minimax
control \(u^\star\) with
\[
r_m(u^\star)\leq V\quad\text{for every }m.
\]
Combining this inequality with (12) yields
\[
V\leq\lambda^{\star\top}r(u^\star)\leq V.
\]
Hence \(u^\star\) is a Bayes best response to \(\lambda^\star\).
Markovization preserves its complete risk vector, so it may be taken Markov
in \((t,X,Q,b^{\lambda^\star})\).  Regard this single response as a finite
mixture of one Bayes best response and put \(u^\epsilon=u^\star\); it is in
fact an exact saddle response, which is stronger than required.

For this finite mixture \(u^\epsilon\), every nature prior \(\lambda\) satisfies
\[
\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon,
\]
whereas (12) gives, for every control \(u\),
\[
\sum_m\lambda_m^\star r_m(u)\geq V.
\]
These are the two \(\epsilon\)-saddle inequalities.  Taking point-mass
\(\lambda\) in the first gives
\(r_m(u^\epsilon)\leq V+\epsilon\) for every scenario.  The construction
uses only the finite-dimensional simplex on the declared arbitrary finite
scenario list and the bound \(|h_j^m|\leq H\); null-boundary closure is
irrelevant.

Write \(\ell_{m,\delta}^-\) and \(\ell_{m,\delta}^+\) for the losses in
Definition~\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\).  The scalar
envelope definitions give, for every \(a\in\mathbb R\),
\[
f_\delta^-(a)\leq\mathbf1\{a<0\}\leq f_\delta^+(a).
\tag{18}
\]
Multiplication by the nonnegative weights
\(w_j\mathbf1\{h_j^m>0\}\), followed by summation, yields
\[
0\leq\ell_{m,\delta}^-\leq\ell_m\leq
\ell_{m,\delta}^+\leq1.
\tag{19}
\]
If \(c_{m,\delta}^\pm\) denotes the oracle value for
\(\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\), taking infima in (19) gives
\[
B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda),
\qquad
c_{m,\delta}^-\leq c_m\leq c_{m,\delta}^+.
\tag{20}
\]
These are bounds on the observed-law design functionals and do not redefine
the causal regret target \(V\).

\emph{A computable regularity modulus.}
Put \(s_k=x_k-q_k/2\) and
\(e_I=|I|^{-1}\sum_{k\in I}\exp(s_k)\).  Along a line segment in
\((x,q)\), either envelope composed with
\(a_j=\min_{I\ni j}e_I-20\) is absolutely continuous.  Wherever its
derivative is nonzero, an active intersection obeys
\[
19<20-\delta\leq e_I\leq20+\delta<21.
\]
At such a point,
\[
\sum_{k\in I}\left|\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial x_k}\right|=e_I<21,
\qquad
\sum_{k\in I}\left|\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial q_k}\right|
=\frac{e_I}{2}<\frac{21}{2}.
\]
Since the envelope slope is at most \(1/\delta\), integration along the
segment gives the conservative bound
\[
|\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x,q)-\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x',q')|
\leq\frac{32}{\delta}\|(x,q)-(x',q')\|_\infty.
\tag{21}
\]
No division by an allocation clock occurs.

For the likelihoods in the frozen core,
\[
d\log Z_m=\sum_jh_j^m\,dx_j-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2\,dq_j.
\]
The bounded-scenario condition gives
\[
|d\log Z_m|\leq K\left(H+\frac{H^2}{2}\right)
\|(dx,dq)\|_\infty.
\]
Differentiating the posterior weights gives
\[
db_m^\lambda=b_m^\lambda\left(d\log Z_m-
\sum_rb_r^\lambda d\log Z_r\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\sum_m|db_m^\lambda|
\leq2K\left(H+\frac{H^2}{2}\right)
\|(dx,dq)\|_\infty.
\tag{22}
\]
This remains true when some prior coordinates vanish.  Combining
(21)--(22), the normalized posterior terminal payoff has modulus
\[
\Omega_\delta(d)=
\min\!\left\{1,
\left(\frac{32}{\delta}
+2K\left(H+\frac{H^2}{2}\right)\right)d\right\}.
\tag{23}
\]
On a guard box, divide the unnormalized reference payoff by a computable
bound \(C_G\geq\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\).  The multiplier lies in \([0,1]\)
and satisfies the same likelihood Lipschitz calculation, so (23) is also a
valid conservative modulus for the scaled datum.

The modulus propagates backward.  Couple two processes started from states
at the same time by using the same future noise and feed the second policy
the first history translated by the initial state difference.  The controls
then coincide and the terminal score-clock difference equals the initial
difference.  Equations (21)--(22) bound the two conditional payoffs.
Taking infima in both directions proves the same modulus for each exact
finite-stage continuation value.  This coupling remains valid when an
allocation coordinate is zero.

\emph{Validated finite recursion.}
Under the zero-drift reference law, bounded predictability makes
\[
Z_m(X(t),Q(t))=
\exp\!\left\{\sum_jh_j^mX_j(t)
-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}
\tag{24}
\]
a mean-one likelihood process.  For a simple predictable control, this
follows by successive Gaussian conditioning.  General controls follow by
stochastic-integral approximation; the integrands are bounded by \(H\), so
the exponential second moments are uniformly bounded.  Hence, for bounded
terminal \(R\),
\[
\mathbb E_m^u[R]=\mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))R].
\tag{25}
\]
Thus the reference-law terminal datum is exactly
\(\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\).

Fix \(\delta\), a finite time partition, and a guard radius \(G>H\).
On \(\|x\|_\infty\leq G\), (24) is at most
\(C_G=\exp(KHG)\).  Divide by \(C_G\).  At first guard exit the scaled
conditional continuation lies in \([0,1]\); this is the exterior interval
used by the algorithm and is not a clamping assertion.

Suppose the vertices \(v\) of a viable state cell carry intervals enclosing
a continuation function \(F\), and \(y\) has multilinear barycentric
weights \(\beta_v\) in that cell.  If its diameter is \(d\), then
\[
\left|F(y)-\sum_v\beta_vF(v)\right|
\leq\sum_v\beta_v\Omega_\delta(\|y-v\|_\infty)
\leq\Omega_\delta(d).
\tag{26}
\]
Therefore the barycentric interval enlarged by \(\Omega_\delta(d)\)
encloses \(F(y)\).

For time increment \(a>0\), constant allocation
\(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\), and standard Gaussian \(z\), the reference
transition is
\[
(x,q)\longmapsto
\bigl(x+(av)^{1/2}\mathbin\odot z,\ q+av\bigr).
\tag{27}
\]
For each retained Gaussian cell, interval arithmetic encloses the entire
image of (27).  Multiplying its nonnegative continuation interval by an
outward-rounded probability interval and summing outward preserves
enclosure; omitted mass is multiplied by \([0,1]\).  Coupling allocations
\(v,v'\) with the same \(z\) and using
\((\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\leq|p-q|\) bounds the control-net error by
\[
\mathbb E\,\Omega_\delta\!\left(
a\|v-v'\|_1+\sqrt{a\|v-v'\|_1}\,\|z\|_2\right).
\tag{28}
\]
Bounded convergence makes (28) tend uniformly to zero with the control-net
radius.  Taking the minimum of lower endpoints minus this error and of upper
endpoints plus this error encloses the Bellman infimum over the whole
simplex.  Backward induction using (26)--(28) proves enclosure at every time
level.  For a fixed time partition and guard box, all interpolation,
control-net, Gaussian-cell, Gaussian-tail, and rounding widths tend to zero
under refinement.  Gaussian cell probabilities have effective rational
outward bounds: integrate rational Taylor bounds for
\(\exp(-z^2/2)\) on bounded cells and use
\(\Pr\{|Z|>z\}\leq2e^{-z^2/2}\) outside the truncation box.

\emph{Passage to continuous time.}
Let \(P_a^v\) denote the Gaussian operator in (27), and set
\[
\mathcal L^v\phi=\frac12\sum_jv_j\partial_{x_jx_j}\phi+
\sum_jv_j\partial_{q_j}\phi.
\tag{29}
\]
For the exact regularized recursion on a partition
\(0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1\), with \(a_l=t_{l+1}-t_l\),
\[
J_l=\min_{v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)}P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1},
\qquad
J_l\leq P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1}\quad\text{for every }v.
\tag{30}
\]
The second relation is the source of a certified lower bound.

Convolve the multilinear lower interpolants on the inner score box with a
rational compactly supported \(C^3\) tensor mollifier of radius \(\kappa\)
whose support lies in the guard box.  Convolution commutes with
\(P_a^v\).  If the one-layer interval error is at most \(\xi_l\),
subtracting \(\sum_{s\geq l}\xi_s\) restores the second inequality in
(30) for the smoothed lower interpolants.  Taylor's formula with integral
remainder gives
\[
P_a^v\phi-\phi-a\mathcal L^v\phi=\mathcal R_a^v(\phi).
\tag{31}
\]
Derivative intervals of the mollified interpolant and truncated Gaussian
moments give outward rational bounds for \(\mathcal R_a^v\).  For fixed
\(\kappa\), the score remainder is bounded by a computable multiple of
\(a^{3/2}\kappa^{-3}\), the clock remainder by a computable multiple of
\(a^2\kappa^{-2}\), and the interpolation contribution by \(\xi_l\).
After division by \(a\), all residuals vanish along rational refinements
satisfying
\[
\max_la_l\downarrow0,\quad
\sum_l\xi_l\downarrow0,\quad
\max_l\frac{\xi_l}{a_l}\downarrow0,\quad
\kappa\downarrow0,\quad
\max_la_l^{1/2}\kappa^{-3}\downarrow0.
\tag{32}
\]
The deterministic nested enumeration contains such tuples and checks these
quantities.  The terminal mollification error is at most
\(\Omega_\delta(\kappa)\).

Linear interpolation in time then gives a computable terminal discrepancy
\(e_T\) and residual \(e_B(t)\geq0\) such that
\[
\phi^-(1,\cdot)\leq C_G^{-1}\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm,
\quad
\phi^-\leq0\ \text{on the guard boundary},
\quad
\partial_t\phi^-+\mathcal L^v\phi^-\geq-e_B(t)
\tag{33}
\]
for every \(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\), with
\[
e_T+\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{34}
\]
For a simple predictable control stopped at guard exit, successive
conditional Gaussian integrations and (31) telescope.  Since
\(\mathcal L^u=\sum_ju_j\mathcal L^{e_j}\), every such control has scaled
risk at least
\[
\phi^-(0,0,0)-\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt.
\tag{35}
\]
All quantities are bounded on the guard box.  Stochastic-integral
approximation therefore extends (35) to every progressively measurable
control.  This proves the lower validation directly, without a global
generalized-terminal comparison theorem.

For the upper side, the grid recursion selects a predictable
piecewise-constant policy, and the independent fixed-policy recursion
encloses its actual risk.  Such policies approximate every admissible
control.  Indeed, predictable simple simplex processes \(v^{(N)}\) can be
chosen with
\[
\mathbb E\int_0^1\|u(t)-v^{(N)}(t)\|_1\,dt\longrightarrow0.
\tag{36}
\]
Using common Brownian motions and the square-root inequality gives
\[
\mathbb E\|Q^u(1)-Q^{v^{(N)}}(1)\|_1\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\sum_j\mathbb E\left|
\int_0^1(\sqrt{u_j(t)}-\sqrt{v_j^{(N)}(t)})\,dW_j(t)
\right|^2\longrightarrow0.
\tag{37}
\]
The drift difference in every scenario is at most \(H\) times the first
quantity.  Equations (21) and (37) therefore imply convergence of every
regularized scenario risk, uniformly over the finite scenario list.
Approximation of the finitely many simple action values by the rational
control net, using (28), completes the upper approximation.  Combining it
with (34)--(35) proves that the two regularized Bellman endpoints converge
to the same continuous-control value.  At a fixed partition, backward
conditioning makes the current score, clock, and likelihood vector a
sufficient Markov state, so the finite recursion searches the required
state-dependent class.  If \(v_j=0\), (27) fixes coordinate \(j\) and
(29) assigns it zero coefficient; hence no forced-exploration premise is
used.

\emph{Guard control.}
Under scenario \(m\),
\[
X_j(t)=h_j^mQ_j(t)+M_j(t),\qquad
M_j(t)=\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),\qquad0\leq Q_j(t)\leq1.
\]
Successive Gaussian conditioning, followed by simple-process
approximation, shows that
\(\exp\{\theta M_j(t)-\theta^2Q_j(t)/2\}\) is a mean-one nonnegative
martingale.  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}howard\mbox{-}linear\mbox{-}boundary}\)
with \(\lambda=b\), \(\beta=e^{-b^2/2}\), and repeat for \(-M_j\).
A union bound and \(|h_j^m|\leq H\) give, uniformly in \(m\) and \(u\),
\[
\Pr_m^u\!\left\{\max_j\sup_{t\leq1}|X_j(t)|>G\right\}
\leq2K\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(G-H)^2}{2}\right\},\qquad G>H.
\tag{38}
\]
Thus exterior continuation intervals affect a risk only through the
explicit probability in (38), which tends to zero as \(G\to\infty\).

\emph{Minimax assembly and termination.}
Define
\[
\mathcal G(\lambda)=B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m
=\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u).
\tag{39}
\]
Because \(r_m(u)\in[0,1]\),
\[
|\mathcal G(\lambda)-\mathcal G(\lambda')|
\leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
\tag{40}
\]
For integer \(D\), the rational simplex net consisting of
\((k_1/D,\ldots,k_M/D)\) with nonnegative integer coordinates summing to
\(D\) contains every point mass and has \(\ell_1\)-radius at most
\(2(M-1)/D\).  Theorem
\(\mathrm{thm{:}least\mbox{-}favorable\mbox{-}saddle}\) gives
\[
V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\mathcal G(\lambda).
\tag{41}
\]
At every prior-net point, (20) gives
\[
B_\delta^-(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^+
\leq\mathcal G(\lambda)\leq
B_\delta^+(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^-.
\tag{42}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}quantitative\mbox{-}terminal\mbox{-}comparison}\), the
regularization width in (42) is at most
\[
\bigl(B_\delta^+-B_\delta^-\bigr)
+\sum_m\lambda_m(c_{m,\delta}^+-c_{m,\delta}^-)
\leq2\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta),
\tag{43}
\]
and \(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta)\to0\).  Equations (40)--(43),
together with the validated point-mass recursions, give certified dual
lower and upper bounds including the oracle offsets.

For the primal bound, a finite mixture with weights \(p_s\) has scenario
risk \(\sum_sp_sL(u_s,m)\).  If the independent fixed-policy recursion gives
risk intervals \([L_m^-,L_m^+]\) and the point-mass recursion gives oracle
intervals \([c_m^-,c_m^+]\), then
\[
V\leq\max_m\{L_m^+-c_m^-\}.
\tag{44}
\]
Thus the recovered-policy upper endpoint is valid independently of the
optimization recursion that selected the mixture.

All lower endpoints converge upward to \(V\) by (34), (38), and
(40)--(43), as the prior radius, terminal width, guard-exit probability,
mesh, cell, tail, and rounding errors vanish.  For the upper endpoints,
take the finite \(\varepsilon\)-saddle mixture of Markov Bayes responses
from \(\mathrm{thm{:}least\mbox{-}favorable\mbox{-}saddle}\).  A net prior
within radius \(r_\lambda\) of its least-favorable prior makes each component
\(2r_\lambda\)-Bayes, because both a fixed policy's Bayes risk and the Bayes
value are \(1\)-Lipschitz in the prior.  Equations (36)--(37) approximate
these finitely many components by enumerated grid policies, which are
eventually retained.  Their mixture is feasible for the rational
scenario-risk linear program, and (38), (43), and the independent recursion
make (44) at most \(V+\varepsilon+o(1)\).  Letting
\(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves downward convergence of the cumulative
primal endpoints to \(V\).

Every candidate computation is finite.  Gaussian probabilities and
elementary functions have terminating rational Taylor enclosures on bounded
cells; omitted tails use (38); and both optimization problems are finite
rational linear programs.  The deterministic enumeration contains
\(\delta\downarrow0\), \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), \(G\uparrow\infty\), and the
nested refinements required by (32).  Therefore its actual ledger sum tends
to zero.  For every \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}>0\), some finite candidate
has certified gap at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\), so the search
reaches it and terminates.  Cumulative maxima of lower endpoints and minima
of independently validated upper endpoints are monotone and retain
validity.  At termination,
\[
\underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon},
\qquad
\overline V_{\varepsilon}-\underline V_{\varepsilon}
\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}},
\]
and the independently evaluated returned mixture obeys
\(\max_mr_m(u)\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}\).

Finally, the gap gives
\(\overline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\).
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}boundary\mbox{-}stable\mbox{-}frontier}\) transfers
the finite mixture's scenario-risk vector to predictable finite-horizon
policies and gives \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\).  Since \(M\) is finite,
\[
\max_mr_{n,m}(\pi_n)=\max_mr_m(u)+o(1)
\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}+o(1).
\]
The proof used only the exact finite scenario list and the bound
\(|h_j^m|\leq H\), so the certificate applies to arbitrary finite bounded
\(\mathcal H_0\) without null-boundary closure.

proposed.statement: For every finite \(\mathcal H_0\subset[-H,H]^K\), the fixed Gaussian grid experiment is exactly embedded by vertex controls in the score diffusion, and the strict extension from the regular-payoff results of Wager and Xu and Adusumilli holds: arbitrary predictable policies, zero-allocation faces, and the discontinuous closed-test terminal loss satisfy \(\sup_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}|B_n(\lambda)-B(\lambda)|\to0\), \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\) for every \(m\), and \(V_n\to V\). Moreover, for each \(\epsilon>0\) there are predictable finite-horizon policies whose scenario-risk vectors converge coordinatewise to that of an \(\epsilon\)-optimal diffusion control.
proposed.justification: It identifies the attainable local-power regret frontier of the fixed confirmatory test for any finite bounded scenario list.
proposed.gap: Existing diffusion transfers cover regular payoffs; this theorem establishes boundary-stable transfer for the discontinuous closed-test loss while allowing legal zero-allocation faces.
proposed.consumer: It converts a continuum recruitment solution into asymptotically valid finite-stage policies for interAdapt-style designs.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof applies to every finite bounded scenario list, so the obsolete null-boundary-closure dependency is removed and the unchanged substantive claim is stated with that scope explicitly.

proposed.statement: For every finite \(\mathcal H_0\subset[-H,H]^K\), the minimax values obey \(V_n=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\{\inf_{\pi_n\in\Pi_n}\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mL_n(\pi_n,m)-\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mc_{n,m}\}\) and \(V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}\{\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mL(u,m)-\sum_{m=1}^M\lambda_mc_m\}\), with attained least-favorable priors. For every \(\epsilon>0\), a finite mixture of Bayes best responses that are Markov in \((t,(X_j(t),Q_j(t))_{j\in\mathcal J},(b_m^\lambda)_{m=1}^M)\) is an \(\epsilon\)-saddle control and has every scenario regret at most \(V+\epsilon\).
proposed.justification: The least-favorable prior converts robust enrichment over any finite bounded scenario list into posterior-state control without mistaking one Bayes rule for a minimax policy.
proposed.gap: Chosen-prior enrichment designs do not construct the adversarial prior or a simultaneous scenario-risk saddle mixture.
proposed.consumer: It supplies robust scenario weights and a policy mixture for a confirmatory trial design specification.

prose_updates.tldr: The novelty-bearing kernel fixes the arithmetic-mean closed e-test and characterizes adaptive subgroup recruitment over an arbitrary finite bounded scenario set through a minimax local-power regret frontier.  A quantitative virtual-score envelope comparison gives boundary-stable transfer for the discontinuous terminal loss while allowing zero-allocation faces; finite-scenario duality then yields least-favorable priors and posterior-state controls.  A deterministic nested interval Bellman search gives convergent monotone lower and upper bounds, validates guard exit, interpolation, Gaussian integration, oracle offsets, and an independently re-evaluated policy mixture, and stops when its actual ledger is within the requested tolerance.  No null-boundary closure, forced exploration, closed-form mesh size, complexity bound, convergence rate, or off-origin terminal comparison is assumed or claimed.  Strong familywise error and simultaneous one-sided confidence sequences remain supporting corollaries.

project_justification.gap: Existing enrichment designs optimize a chosen-prior utility or a discretized two-stage program, and existing adaptive-experiment diffusions transfer regular risk functionals.  They do not characterize minimax regret for the discontinuous rejection vector of a fixed closed e-test over an arbitrary finite bounded scenario list, nor do they provide a validated primitive-input interval certificate for that multidimensional frontier.
project_justification.niche: Holding the confirmatory test and its established error guarantee fixed isolates the recruitment-design question.  The local Gaussian score experiment combines a nonregular terminal decision with an auditable finite-scenario robust-control problem; no closure convention is imposed on the scenario list.
project_justification.fill: The project derives a quantitative boundary-stability modulus, proves value and risk-vector transfer for arbitrary finite bounded scenarios while permitting zero allocations, reduces robust design to a least-favorable posterior-control problem, and proves termination of a deterministic nested certificate search whose candidate-specific interval ledger validates a policy mixture and the limiting minimax value.

prose_updates.related_work: Adusumilli's 2025 Econometrica article provides the nearest Bayes and minimax diffusion-PDE architecture and numerical policy recovery; the present frontier theorem adds boundary-stable transfer for a discontinuous closed-test payoff while permitting zero-allocation controls.  Adusumilli's 2026 allocation-process representation supplies the broad finite-to-continuous experiment donor, while the quantitative closed-test envelope comparison supplies the missing risk-transfer step.  Wager and Xu provide the weak-signal score-clock construction for regular state-dependent randomization.  Burnett and Jennison and Ballarini et al. establish prior-weighted enrichment under frequentist error control; the least-favorable-prior saddle instead targets robust regret over any declared finite bounded scenario list.  Rosenblum, Fang, and Liu inform the finite optimization architecture through a sparse two-stage program, and Baas, ter Schure, and van Rosmalen inform it through scalar e-value dynamic programming.  Neither comparator supplies the present deterministic nested lower-and-upper validation or the independent recovered-policy check, and no complexity separation is claimed.  Vovk and Wang's arithmetic e-merging result together with closed testing yields the fixed strong-familywise-error guarantee as a supporting corollary.  Howard et al.'s time-uniform supermartingale inversion and Ville's inequality yield the simultaneous one-sided subgroup sequences as a supporting corollary.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The common-drift translation and initial-state envelope squeeze do not by themselves prove comparison or uniqueness at every off-origin terminal boundary state.  The value certificate therefore uses direct finite-horizon Bellman enclosure and stopped-process verification for continuous terminal envelopes, not global generalized-terminal Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman uniqueness.  Its termination theorem is qualitative and computable: it searches nested finite rational refinements until the actual ledger closes.  It does not supply a closed-form mesh schedule, arithmetic operation count, or convergence rate.  A nontrivial archived numerical run remains an implementation deliverable rather than a mathematical premise, and the uncertified floating-point presolve value is excluded.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The novelty-bearing results concern known unit Gaussian variance, finitely many prespecified disjoint subgroups, an arbitrary finite scenario set contained in the declared bounded local-effect box, boundary-stable discontinuous-risk diffusion transfer while allowing zero-allocation controls, and a primitive-input deterministic certificate search for the multidimensional frontier.  Null-boundary closure is an optional application convention, not a theorem hypothesis or certificate input.  The certificate guarantees eventual termination at every positive requested tolerance but advertises no closed-form discretization or complexity rate.  Strong familywise error and simultaneous lower confidence sequences are supporting corollaries of cited general results.  Unknown variance, delayed responses, overlapping or data-discovered subgroups, and optimization of the test or its e-alternative are outside scope.  The exact \(K=2,n=1\) reduction is a sanity check; a nontrivial interval-certified worked instance remains an explicit computational deliverable, and global statewise generalized-terminal Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman comparison remains open.
